We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

2611.23673.title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
2611.23673.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

2611.23691.title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
2611.23691.abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

2611.23708.title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
2611.23708.abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.

2611.23716.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
2611.23716.abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

2611.23729.title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
2611.23729.abstract: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.

2611.23732.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
2611.23732.abstract: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

2611.23750.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
2611.23750.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

2611.23753.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
2611.23753.abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.

2611.23825.title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
2611.23825.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

2611.23843.title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
2611.23843.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

2611.23858.title: LAGR: Language-Aware Grasp Re-Ranking for Task Oriented Grasping
2611.23858.abstract: Grasping is a fundamental capability for robotic manipulation, with the appropriate grasp depending on the downstream task. For example, a hammer should be held by its handle for hammering but by its head when it is handed over. Selecting such a grasp requires consideration of two criteria: physical feasibility on the object and suitability for the task. Developing such an approach requires dense grasp labels with both feasibility and task scores on real observations, but existing task-oriented grasping datasets are small, synthetic, or costly to annotate. To address this gap, we construct a dataset of 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations over 100,911 image-task pairs from $17$ object categories. Additionally, we introduce LAGR, a task-oriented grasp detection method that explicitly addresses both these challenges. Given vision-language inputs, LAGR first generates task-independent grasp proposals along with a physical feasibility score, and then scores the generated grasps with a language-conditioned re-ranker that reasons over all proposals jointly. Experiments show that LAGR outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points. We further validate LAGR on real objects by executing task-oriented grasps with a Franka Research 3 robot.

2611.23875.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
2611.23875.abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

2611.23896.title: Kernel Ridge Attention: Nonlinear Memory with Selective Forgetting
2611.23896.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.

2611.23930.title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
2611.23930.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. To mitigate data scarcity and domain gaps, we introduce a fully automated 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based pipeline to generate scalable photorealistic UAV navigation data. A progressive three-stage training strategy further enhances grounding, scene reasoning, and complex navigation. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Finally, we design onboard optimization techniques, including token sparsification and model lightweighting, achieving 7.1x-9.4x speedup while maintaining high navigation performance on resource-limited UAV platforms. Experiments show great improvements over existing methods in both simulation and real-world UAV navigation. Project website: this https URL

2611.23999.title: ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
2611.23999.abstract: Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.

2611.24000.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
2611.24000.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.

2611.24001.title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
2611.24001.abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.

2611.24005.title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
2611.24005.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

2611.24037.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
2611.24037.abstract: Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change. \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. It preserves the original specification as authoritative ground truth and appends confidence-filtered refinements to clarify implicit constraints. \textsc{FormalFixer} uses both intent mismatch and verifier-generated counterexample cone graphs to guide iterative RTL patching. This workflow explicitly checks specification--assertion--RTL correspondence. Results support intent alignment for FPV-based hardware repair.

2611.24052.title: From Data to Valves: A Self-Learning, Production-Grade Edge Stack for Sustainable HVAC Control
2611.24052.abstract: Learned HVAC controllers rarely leave the simulator, and those that do are typically trained offline, frozen at deployment and retrained from the cloud. We present a production stack in which three learning components run on one NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway per building, adapt continuously from the building's own data, and verify their own effect. (a) A compact transformer-encoder forecaster, one per equipment group with learned per-unit embeddings, predicts every air-side unit's next-cycle temperature and learns prequentially, one gradient step per five-minute cycle, behind five independent gates that bound the influence of any corrupt reading. (b) A distributional soft actor-critic agent, one shared policy across unit types, converts the measured state into a chilled-water valve position under a structural safety envelope that no learned component can soften; its second generation learns nightly on the device from recorded transitions alone, with a behaviour anchor and critic calibration terms, is scored by four model-free metrics and promoted by atomic hot-swap. (c) A change-point regression baseline held to ASHRAE Guideline 14 supplies the counterfactual against which savings are certified. On eighteen months of data from a hotel the forecaster converges from random weights within a week and reaches 0.37, 0.39 and 0.11 degree C MAE for air-handling, fresh-air and fan-coil units with no retraining event; on a different hotel the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period to within 0.07%. The RL agent has completed its in-simulator campaign and runs in shadow on 104 units; we report measured latency and memory of every service on a shared 15 GB device, the systems lessons of the campaign, and precisely what the evidence does and does not yet establish.

2611.24055.title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
2611.24055.abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.

2611.24059.title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
2611.24059.abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

2611.24085.title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
2611.24085.abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, covering 17 model--precision combinations across 4 LLM families. On Qwen deployments, LEDGE achieves request-level mean absolute percentage errors below 3.6% and a 135.3 times aggregate speedup over physical inference. Performance model calibrated on one LLM family yield 7.44% zero-shot end-to-end latency MAPE across three other families. Further simulations show how shared-link contention affects placement decisions and network topology constrains scaling. Across four edge environments, LEDGE completes 26,773 simulation runs in 83.8 minutes, enabling efficient exploration of deployment strategies under diverse resource conditions and serving objectives. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

2611.24114.title: The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
2611.24114.abstract: This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.

2611.24156.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
2611.24156.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

2611.24168.title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning
2611.24168.abstract: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at this https URL.

2611.24208.title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
2611.24208.abstract: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.

2611.24214.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
2611.24214.abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

2611.24231.title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
2611.24231.abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.

2611.24313.title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
2611.24313.abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.

2611.24377.title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
2611.24377.abstract: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.

2611.24394.title: Temporal Rank in Recurrent Neural Networks
2611.24394.abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a natural framework for temporal modelling, yet are often dismissed due to their sequential, non-parallelisable computation and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies, typically attributed to vanishing and exploding gradients. We identify a distinct and under-explored limitation: an information bottleneck induced by rank-constrained hidden state dynamics, which limits the number of independent input directions that can be preserved over time, as reflected in the rank of the input-to-state mapping. We show that this constraint restricts temporal capacity independently of gradient stability. To address this, we introduce structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal separability and prevent saturation of the input-to-state Jacobian over time. On controlled sequence tasks, the resulting model exhibits rapid learning despite remaining strictly within a standard RNN formulation. Our results demonstrate that RNN performance is governed by the evolution and preservation of temporal rank, and suggest that mitigating gradient pathologies alone is insufficient without explicitly maintaining temporal capacity.

2611.24413.title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
2611.24413.abstract: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.

2611.24428.title: Keeping Shielded Data-Driven Controllers Safe Under System Evolution via Model Consistency
2611.24428.abstract: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) increasingly contain data-driven controllers, which raise safety concerns given their black-box nature. A common mitigation is to enforce system safety via a shield around the controller, which restricts the inputs based on assumptions about the physical system. However, these assumptions are usually fixed and may become invalid as the system evolves (during development or due to component degradation), possibly leading to unsafe behavior. We address this limitation in a model-driven approach that treats both the data-driven controller and safety shield as first-class models that are integrated into a virtual single underlying model (V-SUM) alongside system models. We describe system evolution as changes in the associated models, such that consistency checking yields a continuous assessment of safety guarantees. In case of inconsistencies, consistency-preservation rules automatically update the models and restore a valid safety shield. We evaluate our approach on a reach-avoid task for a unicycle system. The results show that consistency-driven evolution effectively maintains safety guarantees under system changes and provides a principled basis for evaluating and restoring performance.

2611.24453.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
2611.24453.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: this https URL.

2611.24475.title: Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams
2611.24475.abstract: Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.

2611.24489.title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
2611.24489.abstract: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.

2611.24491.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
2611.24491.abstract: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit this http URL prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.

2611.24496.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
2611.24496.abstract: GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

2611.24522.title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking
2611.24522.abstract: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

2611.24540.title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
2611.24540.abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.

2611.24598.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
2611.24598.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.

2611.24609.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
2611.24609.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

2611.24641.title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
2611.24641.abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.

2611.24699.title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Québec French
2611.24699.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Québec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Québec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.

2611.24711.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
2611.24711.abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

2611.24728.title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
2611.24728.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

2611.24763.title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
2611.24763.abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

2611.24764.title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
2611.24764.abstract: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

2611.24765.title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
2611.24765.abstract: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.

2611.24782.title: Learning Trajectories Leave Decodable Traces in Neural Network Weight Space and Internal Representations
2611.24782.abstract: Neural networks trained on the same task develop related weight-space structures, yet remain distinguishable after learning. Do these differences merely reflect alternative solutions, or do they preserve information about individual learning histories? We tested whether final weights reveal initialization, task order, and earlier trajectory states. Training reorganized the ensemble: initial pairwise distances did not consistently predict final distances. Nevertheless, all 30 trained networks were correctly matched to their initial weights among ten candidates per dataset. Networks sharing an initialization also developed recognizable final hidden representations across different batch schedules, although direct comparisons with initial activity did not recover identity.
